newsitem.title: GERMANY: Coffee roaster KJS to maintain policy on stocks.
newsitem.headline: Coffee roaster KJS to maintain policy on stocks.

text.p: Current tightness in coffee markets is no reason for processors to seek huge stock additions during periods of lower prices, Kraft Jacobs Suchard (KJS) chairman Bernhard Huber said.
"We have never really operated a just-in-time strategy," he said in response to questions at a news conference on the group's 1996 results.
"Our cover varies between supply for a few months or less."
KJS is part of Philip Morris Inc.
Huber said most roasters had misjudged the emerging coffee market crisis earlier in 1997, and now faced an explosion of raw material costs.
But the price surge had even baffled KJS buyers with 30 years experience in the market because it was not based on weather-induced crop fundamentals, he said.
A quality drive in the U.S. coffee market might have contributed to an unprecented tightness in top arabicas, which are typically used in German blends.
Finance director Udo Hollstein said KJS would manage fluctuations in operating costs via ex-plant coffee prices.
It would not become a long holder of coffee again -- as it did in 1977, when a sharp and sudden collapse of the market cost the company 100 million marks.
Huber added the company would "under no circumstance" interfere with the quality of its roasted coffee.
